packs.title: Gainesville’s galleries and green places
packs.promise: Art, working landscapes and small discoveries across the city.

q.s: Make an original page from an exterior silhouette.
st: Choose an open, dry visitor-path viewpoint that leaves the entrance and bridge clear. Return if event signs restrict the approach.
Notice one rising edge in the building and one lower edge in the surrounding trees or path. Describe their directions without tracing decorative designs.
Create a small original composition with three abstract marks: one rising, one resting and one connecting them. A written arrangement of the marks also works.
Give your composition a short title and explain which observed edge prompted it. Keep the page with you.

q.s: Build a small evidence chain inside a nature center.
st: Enter the actually opened public nature-center exhibit area. Find three available pieces of interpretation connected to the local watershed, living things or cultural history.
For each, note a visible detail and paraphrase one fact in your own words. If a relationship is unclear, record a question rather than guessing.
Arrange your three notes into a chain: place, living thing and human choice, or another connection the actual exhibits support.
Write one sentence explaining the strongest connection and identify which exhibit evidence supports it. Notes after exit are valid.

q.t: A page from a forest edge
q.s: Translate present-day growth into an original pattern.
st: From a permitted dry path, choose three visibly different kinds of line in the growth around you: branching, narrow, rounded or words of your own.
Draw three original marks for those lines, or describe the marks in words. Leave all plants undisturbed.
Use the city’s account of a former horse farm becoming forest to write one question about how a landscape changes. Do not infer an exact plant age or species.
Arrange your marks into a small pattern and add the question beneath it. Keep your own page; no landscape material is collected.

packs.title: Gainesville’s downtown and nearby places
packs.promise: Two afternoons of history, invention and public-space discoveries.

q.s: Follow a small subject through public browsing cues.
st: Enter the actually opened public browsing area and choose a small subject that interests you, without signing in or using restricted collections.
Find three available public cues connected to that subject: a shelf category, a book’s exterior information or a public service sign can each count.
Record each cue in your own words and explain how it could help you begin learning. Do not copy pages or record another visitor’s activity.
Arrange the cues into a first step, a second step and a question still open. Keep your short plan; no loan or account is required.

q.s: Compare two hands-on encounters inside a creativity museum.
st: After admission, enter the actually opened public exhibits and choose two available hands-on activities that staff and posted rules permit for ordinary visitors.
Before trying each, write a small prediction. Try it as directed and record one result or visible change; use an available observation-based exhibit if hands-on access is restricted.
Compare the two encounters and revise one prediction in light of what happened. Explain the actual observation that changed it.
Keep two prediction-and-result notes plus your revision. Notes after exit earn full credit, with no venue photograph or specific outcome required.

q.s: Use a bounded promenade segment to read a route twice.
st: At the open west-side public path, choose and record a fixed starting cue, staying clear of other path users.
Walk an open dry segment for no more than three minutes and identify two fixed cues that would help someone return. Turn sooner for closures, conditions or comfort.
Retrace the same segment to the starting cue. Explain how one cue is easier or harder to recognize from the opposite direction.
Write a short return description using your cues. Distance and speed are not scored, and no water-edge viewpoint is required.
